extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, painters, architects, and students of aesthetics and rhetorical style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for producing sublime (and beautiful) effects in descriptive writing and the visual arts by invoking causes such as power, privation, vastness, infinity, light/darkness, sound, difficulty, and magnificence. Useful for crafting elevated poetic, narrative, or pictorial passages that aim to elicit awe, terror, or reverential feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength and power are sources of the sublime when they evoke terror and contempt rather than merely usefulness; power that is subservient and useful (e.g., a plough-horse) is not sublime, whereas free, uncontrollable, or dangerous strength (lions, tigers, unicorn, leviathan, sovereign authority, or the Deity) produces sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise independence, fury, or uncontrollability rather than usefulness; heighten sublime effect by associating power with terror and contempt. Examples: the wild ass in Job, unicorn and leviathan passages, the awe inspired by sovereigns, and the imaginative response to the Divine ('we shrink into the minuteness of our own nature'). Note tensions: power coupled with benevolence reduces but does not remove terror; present power through sensible images (acts/exertions) rather than abstract attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privation
rubrics_metrics.description: General privations—vacuity, darkness, solitude, and silence—are great because they are terrible and thus cause the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinations of these privations to heighten dread and religious horror; Virgil's mouth of hell passages and Milton/Dryden translations illustrate assembling darkness, silence, and emptiness before revealing great or terrible scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vastness
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness of dimension (extent or quantity) is a powerful cause of the sublime; extension in height or depth often strikes more than mere length, and perpendicularity and rugged/broken surfaces are more effective than smoothness or horizontal extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer height/depth and perpendicular elements to long horizontal spreads; broken, rugged surfaces produce stronger effects. Note that extremes of littleness (minute divisibility) can also astonish the imagination in a way akin to vastness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinity tends to fill the mind with a 'delightful horror' that is the truest test of the sublime. Though few things are truly infinite, things that appear boundless to the senses produce similar effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create the impression of limitless extension or indefinite continuation so imagination meets no perceptible bounds. Use repetition, uniform continuation, or arrangements that prevent the eye from fixing a boundary. The artificial infinite (see Succession and Uniformity) is a practical route to this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession and Uniformity (artificial infinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession (continuation of parts in one direction) and uniformity (unchanging repeated parts) together constitute the artificial infinite and allow bounded objects to take on the character of infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange repeated, uniform parts so the imagination is not checked by variation; examples: rotunds, ranges of uniform pillars, long aisles. Avoid changes in figure, disposition, or colour that break the series. Architectural implications: prefer parallelogram/continuous arrangements over cross-shaped plans which interrupt progression and break perspective; too many angles harm grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude in Building
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness of dimension in architecture is requisite to produce the sublime; small numbers of parts cannot excite an idea of infinity, and manner alone cannot compensate for small dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance height and length—excessive length reduces perceived height via perspective and can weaken effect; use moderate long colonnades/avenues rather than extreme distances. A skilled designer should achieve grand designs by deceptive (artful) means rather than mere huge scale; find a medium between excessive and insufficient magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity in Pleasing Objects
rubrics_metrics.description: A kind of infinity contributes to pleasure in agreeable objects: incompleteness or the promise of more (spring, young animals, unfinished sketches) pleases because imagination anticipates further development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce suggestion or partial completion to engage the imagination with expectation rather than full closure; unfinished or suggestive treatment can be more pleasing than full finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty—when a work appears to have required immense force and labour—is a source of grandeur; the perception of the effort involved creates a grand idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the scale of labour or the daunting means required to produce something (e.g., Stonehenge's huge rude masses), and sometimes rudeness (lack of artifice) increases this feeling by excluding the idea of dexterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: A great profusion of splendid or valuable things creates magnificence and can be a source of the sublime; number and apparent disorder (which suggests an appearance of infinity) augment grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use profusion cautiously—too much splendour or confused abundance can destroy usefulness and taste. To produce magnificence successfully, one must make disorder convey infinity; fire-works and certain poetic descriptions (e.g., starry heaven, rich panegyrics) exemplify effective magnificence. Avoid mere disorder without an appearance of boundlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light
rubrics_metrics.description: Light, considered with its opposites, can produce the sublime only when attended with special circumstances; mere light is too common, but extreme light (overpowering the eye like the sun) or very rapid light (lightning) is grand. A quick transition from light to darkness or vice versa has great effect. Darkness is more productive of sublime ideas than light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit extreme luminance, velocity of light, or sharp transitions; darkness around the Deity ('With the majesty of darkness round / Circles his throne') is a powerful device. Extreme light can function as darkness by overwhelming the senses—use paradoxical extremes to avoid mediocrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light in Building
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings intended to produce the sublime ought to be dark and gloomy because darkness affects the passions more strongly and offers a striking contrast from open-air light; at night the rule reverses (bright illumination produces grandeur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interiors darker than exterior daylight to create a powerful transition; at night, use strong illumination to similar dramatic ends. Make the transition as striking as is consistent with architecture's uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour considered as productive of the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour contributes to the sublime when it is of sad, fuscous tones (black, brown, deep purple) rather than soft or cheerful colours; gay or gaudy drapery is unfit for grand images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pale/cheerful colours and excessive gilding, mosaics, painting, or statues when aiming for the highest sublimity; use melancholic, somber colours for uniformity of striking sublimity. Exception: when uniform high sublimity is not the goal, draw sublimity from other sources but avoid anything light and riant that deadens taste for the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and Loudness
rubrics_metrics.description: Loud sounds (cataracts, raging storms, thunder, artillery) and the shouting of multitudes can overpower the soul, suspend action, and fill the mind with terror—thus producing sublime effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overwhelming loudness or mass vocal sound to amaze and confound imagination; technical musical niceties are unnecessary—raw volume and force suffice for the sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden beginning or cessation of a strong sound rouses attention and produces terror; sudden transitions between extremes do not cause terror, but abrupt unexpected events do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sudden, strong auditory events or a single repeated strong stroke with intervals (e.g., the striking of a great clock in the silence of night) to create an awful, grand effect. Repetition after intervals can reinforce grandeur.
